title: Mothering Sunday
hook: in Britain and Ireland, mid-Lent: a day to visit the mother church and your mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation, kept nine months before Christmas, and your line was nine months to go.

A young woman walks a country lane early on a Sunday in spring, in her one good dress, with wildflowers picked from the hedge. She works as a servant in a big house miles away, and this is one of the few days a year she's let go home. She'll go to the church where she was baptized, then to her mother's door. That's the scene tradition paints of this day in Britain and Ireland, in the middle of Lent, when the fast eased for one Sunday and people went back to where they came from. Today it's mostly cards and flowers. Underneath is an older idea of who your mother is.

In the middle of Lent's long weeks, the Western church kept a Sunday with a lighter tone. Its old opening words came from Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all ye that love her." And in the English prayer book, the letter read that Sunday came from Galatians, where Paul writes: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all." Jerusalem as a mother. The church as a mother. So the first mothering, tradition says, was going back to your mother church: the church where you were baptized, or the great church of your area. People who had moved away came home for it, and then, naturally, went home to their actual mothers too. The custom grew warm edges. Servants were given the day. Children picked flowers on the walk. Some families baked a rich fruit cake, allowed in the eased fast. Over time the church side faded for some families and the mother side stayed: cards, flowers and phone calls home. Some confuse it with the American Mother's Day, which began separately; this one grew from a Sunday in the church year. The old custom sets two things side by side: a place that made you, and a person who made you. The answer to both was the same: a walk down the lane, flowers from the hedge, and a knock at the door.

In your mind, walk the road home, street by street, to a door where someone mothered you: your mother's, a grandmother's, an aunt's, a neighbor's, a friend's mom who fed you, whichever you can walk up to gladly. Let one kindness from that house come back, a plate set down, a coat buttoned. If you pray, name her before God on the step; if not, simply stand there with her a moment.
Mothering Sunday. A Sunday in the middle of Lent when people in Britain and Ireland went back to their mother church, and then to their mothers.
Your line: go home. Any door you can walk up to gladly. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Is Mothering Sunday just the British version of Mother's Day?
options: No. It began as a mid-Lent Sunday for going back to your mother church.
Yes. Britain moved the American day to spring to fit around Easter.
No. It's a Catholic feast honoring Mary, the mother of Jesus.
chat.meaning: Tradition says people went back to their mother church in mid-Lent, then to their mothers. The American Mother's Day began separately.
